nm_santa_fe_area.blurb: Climbing around Santa Fe, in north-central New Mexico, is mostly bolted. Diablo Canyon dominates, with cracked basalt cliffs on both sides of a dry canyon near the Rio Grande, offering sport and multi-pitch routes. The Pecos, northeast of town, has granite sport climbing in a shaded valley, Rats Peak is conglomerate, and Apache Canyon has overhanging sandstone boulders. Routes are mostly 5.10 to 5.13, with 5.11 and 5.12 the heart of it, plus a smaller supply of moderates and a modest amount of trad. Diablo and Cochiti suit the colder months because their cliffs catch sun, and summer climbers head for the Pecos or shadier walls.

co_big_thompson_canyon.blurb: Big Thompson Canyon follows US 34 between Loveland and Estes Park, with granite and gneiss crags visible from the road. Sport and trad are about equally common, with a few top-rope lines, a little bouldering and a small amount of ice. Palisade Mountain is the largest single area, the Narrows and Mary's Bust hold more crags along the road, and the Monastery is a side-road crag with a dense collection of steep faces and slabs. Grades run from 5.7 to 5.12, with the bulk between 5.9 and 5.11 and a handful of 5.13s. Some rock is solid and some is suspect, so judgement matters.

nm_los_alamos_white_rock.blurb: Los Alamos and White Rock sit on the Pajarito Plateau, where canyons have cut through soft volcanic tuff that is too weak to climb. The climbing is on the basalt cliffs within and below it. White Rock is the largest area, with short approaches and a mix of toprope, bolted lead and crack lines. The Dungeon has steep, overhanging sport routes with many 5.12s, and Los Alamos Crags mixes trad, sport and boulders. Trad and sport are both well represented, with a good number of top-ropes and boulders. Grades cluster between 5.9 and 5.12, with a good supply of moderates below that. Town sits at about 6,750 feet.

ca_alabama_hills.blurb: The Alabama Hills are a scatter of coarse, orange-brown granite towers and outcrops on the Lone Pine side of the Sierra, with the Sierra Crest in view. Most routes are bolted sport faces with short approaches, and trad, top-rope and a little bouldering fill out the rest. Alabama Hills North is the biggest section, followed by Alabama Hills South and the smaller Tuttle Creek area. Rock quality varies, and north-facing walls often have good patina while other rock is loose. The grades are friendly: lots of 5.6 to 5.10, a peak around 5.10, and few lines above 5.11. Steeper, harder sport routes have been added more recently.

wi_south.blurb: Southern Wisconsin climbing is a set of scattered sandstone sites, and bouldering is by far the main event. Governor Dodge State Park is the giant of the group, a large park of steep hills, valleys and lakes holding hundreds of boulder problems, plus a small sport bluff. The rock is soft in places and crumbly formations are best avoided. Donald Park, Blackhawk Lake, Fishin' Crag and Wyalusing add more small bluffs and boulders, and there is a little ice. Boulder problems run from V0 into the V8 range, most between V1 and V4. Roped climbs are few, mostly between 5.8 and 5.12, with a small sport and trad base.

az_sedona_area.blurb: Sedona sits on the southern edge of the Colorado Plateau, just south of Flagstaff, and the climbing is a collection of sandstone spires and towers scattered through town and canyons. Trad overwhelmingly dominates, with a smaller sport and top-rope offering and very little bouldering. The rock is often soft and route quality can be inconsistent, so it rewards careful gear placements. The region splits into Sedona proper, West Sedona and the Village of Oak Creek, with a small amount of basalt climbing at higher elevations. Grades are mostly 5.9 to 5.11, with 5.10 the single biggest group and a steady supply of 5.11 and 5.12 for stronger climbers.
